text: Ten years later, every Borders store was closed. About eleven thousand people lost their jobs.
I'm Sam. This is Last Receipt. Tonight, what happened to Borders, the bookstore that outsourced the internet.
Here's the thing. In the eighties, Borders was a bookstore with a data advantage. Hold onto that. It's the saddest part of this story.
Now watch this. Borders gave Amazon its online customers. Every one of them. Their emails, their orders, their habits. And Amazon learned more about Borders' customers than Borders did.
The company that won by knowing which book each store would sell handed that knowledge to its rival.
Here's the hard part. Every one of those bets looked reasonable at the time. Music was big. Leases were cheap. The trouble is they all pointed backward.
Each store stocking the books its own neighbourhood wants. Does that sound familiar? It's what Borders did in 1975.
So what killed Borders? Amazon, of course. Everybody says Amazon.
But Borders didn't lose to the internet. It outsourced it. It took the one thing it was best at, knowing its customers, and gave it to the company that would replace it.
The lesson is short. Never outsource the part of your business that's going to matter most in ten years. Even if it's losing money today.
